newsitem.title: USA: Saudi bombing suspect deported to the United States.
newsitem.headline: Saudi bombing suspect deported to the United States.

text.p: A Saudi man sought by the FBI for questioning about the 1996 truck bombing that killed 19 U.S. airmen in Saudi Arabia arrived in Washington under guard on Tuesday after being deported from Canada, a high-ranking U.S. official said.

The official said a plane carrying the suspect, Hani Abdel-Rahim Hussein al-Sayegh, who was escorted by FBI agents after leaving an Ottawa prison, arrived at an airport in the Washington, D.C., area on on Tuesday night.

U.S. officials said Sayegh, who may have important information about those responsible for the massive bombing, would be held in jail until an initial court apperance before a federal judge on Wednesday afternoon.
They said another hearing had been set for Thursday in which Sayegh would plead guilty to conspiracy charges involving an unrelated attack plotted in the Middle East, but never carried out.

As part of the plea deal that has been reached, Sayegh would plead guilty to the lesser charges and in return would cooperate with U.S. authorities and tell them what he knows about the Khobar Towers bombing last June, the officials said.
The conspiracy charge concerned an aborted attack against the United States that was plotted about six months before the Khobar Towers bombing, the officials said.
Sayegh, 29, a Shi'ite Moslem, has been identified in Canadian court documents as the driver of a car that gave the go-ahead signal for the bomb-laden truck involved in the attack on Khobar Towers.
FBI agents since March have sought to question Sayegh about the June attack on the compound that housed U.S. military personnel in Dhahran in eastern Saudi Arabia.

Sayegh's New York-based lawyer, Michael Wildes, a former federal prosecutor, issued a statement that his client feared for his life if he had been returned to Saudi Arabia, where Sayegh's wife and two daughters still live.

Of the sealed agreement with the U.S. government, Wildes said, "I believe that the arrangement serves both the interests of protecting my client's safety and the U.S. government's interest in investigating the Khobar Towers bombing."

U.S. officials for months have been seeking independent verification of allegations by Saudi Arabia that Iran was behind the attack. Iran has denied any involvement. The FBI has yet to interview any witnesses or suspects in the bombing.

Canadian documents said Sayegh was a member of the radical Saudi Hizbollah (Party of God). Sayegh has claimed he had no involvement in the attack, though sources close to him said he may know others who were involved.
A source in Canada said Sayegh would take a lie-detector test concerning his claim he was not involved in the attack.

Sayegh was arrested last March under a Canadian warrant alleging that he was a "security risk to Canada." But it was not known until this week that he would be sent to the United States instead of Saudi Arabia.
